newsitem.title: USA: Bruised forex pros warily revisit yen carry trade.
newsitem.headline: Bruised forex pros warily revisit yen carry trade.

text.p: Most global bond markets still offer fat yield spreads versus Japan's and tantalize investors even after a sudden yen revaluation scorched speculators in recent days, U.S. players said.
U.S. 10-year Treasury notes currently pay 6.75 percent, a whopping 400 basis points over comparable Japanese government bonds and a powerful incentive to sell the yen for the dollar, experts said.
With short-term Japanese rates under 1.0 percent, investors continue to reap big profits by selling Japanese securities short and investing the cash in more generous paper elsewhere.

"It's so tempting, because interest rates are so low in Japan and relatively high in the U.S. For what appeared to be a minimal amount of currency risk, you can get a preferred return," said David DeRosa, a managing partner at Greenwich, Conn. hedge fund Quadrangle Investments LLC.

But that apparently low-risk play, called the yen-carry trade, abruptly boomeranged with a spectacular 12-percent dollar/yen decline in May, reminding investors that currency markets have two-way traffic that sometimes runs over people.

"As soon as the dollar started to weaken, the corporates and real-money accounts in Japan started to hedge their dollar exposure by selling dollars forward. The hedge funds got crushed," said Richard Gilhooly, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.
The greenback had steadily risen from its post-World War II low at 79.75 yen in April 1995 to as high as 127.47 earlier this month.

But murmurings of higher interest rates in Japan, while the Federal Reserve drew heavy complaints for raising U.S. rates and Japanese officials repeatedly hinted the dollar was unacceptably high dropped the greenback as low as 111.98 yen.
Bond markets have weakened across the globe, underscoring the cornucopia of investments that had been funded with cheap yen-based borrowings, analysts said.

"A lot of people are in that trade -- retail investors in Japan, institutions in Japan, traders in Europe and the U.S., hedge funds, investment managers, private individuals," DeRosa said. "It all came down like a house of cards."
Bond markets slumped across Europe on Thursday, and the yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond backed up to 7.00 percent for the first time since April 28.
But with the dollar stabilizing near 115 yen in recent sessions, analysts said the lure of those fat yields may again overpower fears of currency backlash.
"I would suspect those trades could be put back on," said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Securities Inc. "The dollar is probably off its worst levels against the yen."
Yet the greenback could also resume its downward spiral if fresh signs of a narrowing interest rate gap or U.S. stock market weakness appear, analysts said.
Major U.S. stock averages like the Dow Jones industrials and the Nasdaq composite remain near record highs. Should they back off sharply, the dollar could face a new slump.
"A large part of the (yen-leveraged) positions is in U.S. stocks. If they start to fall heavily, I think you'll see more of the (dollar) unwind coming," said Gilhooly.

With huge sums of money parked in dollars and dollar assets, analysts said current dollar holders could do little to stop further carnage, even the large hedge funds often credited with driving the market for short periods.
"It's hard to fight something when you're losing money and you're getting margin calls," Gilhooly said. "If they try to fight it, they're going to get carried out."
